transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-27
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Location: Zoom
Notes: deep dive on 128k+ long context performance, chunking, KV cache, batching, quantization, and VPC/on-prem considerations; AE+SE here from Redwood; customer side: CTO, ML Lead, Infra.

Summary (auto):
- Focus on supporting 128k+ token contexts for AcmeAnalytics ingestion and retrieval workflows; tradeoffs between latency and throughput discussed; recommended chunking and attention strategies; plan to run benchmark and share configs.

Topics: long-context (128k+), chunking/segmentation, attention optimizations (sparse/chunked attention), KV cache behavior at extreme lengths, batching strategies, quantization tradeoffs, VPC/on-prem kernel tuning, fallback/rollout strategy for Dedicated.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. Quick intros?
[00:06] Rajiv (Acme): Rajiv here, CTO. Tara's our ML lead, Ben is infra. Thanks for doing this deep dive.
[00:12] Carlos (Redwood SE): Hey all, Carlos from Redwood infra team - we'll get into the runtime stuff. Lina will jump on the quantization bits later.
[00:20] Tara (Acme): Hi, quick context - our use case is legal/medical ingestion, 100s of docs per user, want full history queries across months, so we need 128k+ window in some flows. Latency target interactive: p50 < 700ms for short queries, but for long retrievals we can accept up to 2.5s. Throughput matters for batch re-ranking jobs.
[00:38] Maya: Got it. That's helpful. Quick qual: where do you plan to run - hosted API, dedicated, or private VPC?
[00:44] Ben (Acme): We're leaning private - data residency + HIPAA. Might start with Redwood Dedicated for perf baseline then move to Private on prem-ish.
[00:52] Maya: Cool. We'll discuss Dedicated -> Private migration patterns and what to expect.

[00:57] [00:57] Carlos: jumping in - at 128k the main vectors are attention memory, KV cache growth, and I/O for chunking. There are two common approaches we recommend: 1) sparse/chunked attention + sliding window KV cache for active context, and 2) intelligent chunking at retrieval time so you only attend to candidate chunks.
[01:16] Tara: When you say sliding KV, does that mean we evict older keys aggressively? How do you keep coherence for long-range references?
[01:23] Carlos: Yeah, so 'sliding' is a bit overloaded. Practically we keep a hot KV region for the last N tokens (configurable) and either keep summaries or compressed KV entries for older context. For exact cross-document references, we rely on retrieval + re-attend to the specific chunk; that's cheaper than trying to keep every token in the KV at full precision.
[01:42] Simone (Acme): Are summaries auto-generated? We're worried about hallucination drift when compressing.
[01:47] Lina (Redwood): Good question. Summaries are usually task-specific. We can provide a few strategies: 1) vector embeddings + retrieval + local re-attend; 2) lossy summary tokens with lower precision (and controlled temperature); 3) hierarchical chunking where top-level summaries point to chunks. For regulated content we recommend retrieval+re-attend to avoid drift.
[02:07] [02:07] Carlos: On batching: continuous batching helps throughput but can increase tail latency. For interactive flows you want smaller micro-batches, dynamic batching thresholds, and timeouts (e.g., 5-8ms) tuned to your latency SLOs. For bulk re-ranking runs, switch to large batch mode and higher throughput profiles.
[02:26] Rajiv: Can you quantify - what's p50/p95 for a 128k re-attend to 6 chunks (each ~8k) vs naive full-attend?
[02:34] Carlos: Rough order: naive full-attend at 128k is both memory- and compute-bound - latencies explode (several seconds to tens of seconds depending on model size). Our optimized chunked re-attend + KV caching for 6 chunks typically sits in the 400ms-1.2s range p50-p95 on a 4xA100 Dedicated pod with Atlas-quantized runtimes. Naive full-attend can go >5s p95. These are rough - we should run your workload for precise numbers.
[02:56] Tara: You said Atlas-quantized - is that Redwood's quantization profile?
[03:00] Lina: Small typo there from the transcript - we refer to our quant profiles (we have q4_0, q4_kv, q5 etc) and some internal labels like "Atlas" for specific 128k-optimized configs. We'll send the exact config names. q4_kv preserves KV precision to avoid degradation in long context.
[03:18] Ben: On the Private deployment side - how much tuning at kernel level is required? We want to bring our own H100s later.
[03:25] Carlos: If you're on H100s, kernel selection and cuBLAS/cuDNN versions matter. We'll want to run a kernel-selection sweep in your environment; typically it's a quick set of perf runs (we'll do microbenchmarks) to pick the best matmul/attention kernels and memory alloc strategies. Expect 1-2 days of hands-on work.
[03:44] Ben: Good. For KV cache memory at 128k, how much RAM/GPU VRAM are we looking at per active session?
[03:51] Carlos: Depends on model size and whether you keep full KV. Rule-of-thumb: full-precision KV grows linearly - for a 7B-ish model you might be fine keeping multiple minutes of context. For 70B, KV can be tens of GBs. With q4_kv or compressing KV, we can reduce VRAM footprint by ~2-3x. We'll give a modeled estimate for your model variant.
[04:12] [04:12] Tara: What about chunking strategies? We're doing doc-level chunks vs sliding windows - which is better?
[04:18] Carlos: Doc-level is simpler and aligns with retrieval; sliding windows help for streaming or when documents don't align with semantic boundaries. Tradeoff: sliding gives better local coherence but more KV churn. Our recommended hybrid: chunk by doc/section (8k tokens), then maintain a short sliding hot window for the immediate conversation.
[04:36] Rajiv: How do you handle attention optimizations - sparse attention, local+global patterns?
[04:41] Carlos: We support a few approaches: windowed attention for local tokens + global tokens for special indices; block-sparse attention for long-range patterns; and routing-style methods. Many open models now ship with attention optimizations that we leverage. For 128k, the combination of chunking + block-sparse attention gives the best perf/cost balance.
[05:02] Simone: Any model compatibility issues? We intend to use an open large model variant but not sure which.
[05:07] Lina: We maintain a model catalog and verify long-context compatibility. Some models that are not architected for long-range attention will degrade. We'll run an onboarding eval and highlight incompatibilities.
[05:18] [05:18] Ben: Quantization - how risky is it for long-context semantics?
[05:22] Lina: Quantization can affect generation quality, especially in dense attention patterns. For KV we recommend preserving higher precision (q4_kv) or mixed quantization (weights quantized, KV maintained at higher fidelity). We also recommend running your prompt suite and an eval harness - Redwood Optimize can automate regression checks against your criteria.
[05:44] Tara: Do you have any recommended eval metrics specific to long-context?
[05:48] Carlos: Yes: recall of referenced facts across long spans, hallucination rate on retrieval tasks, end-to-end latency, and cost per call. Also structural metrics like chunk boundary hit-rate (how often retrieval picked correct chunk) and KV eviction impact.
[06:02] [06:02] Rajiv: For the private/VPC deploy, where does the control plane live? We need SSO/SAML and audit logs.
[06:08] Maya: For Private we offer a customer-managed control plane option: control plane can be in your VPC or managed with private connectivity. We support SAML SSO, RBAC, and can configure audit logs shipped to your SIEM. We'll share the security checklist.
[06:22] Simone: Any compliance for HIPAA?
[06:24] Maya: Yes, we have a HIPAA+SOC2 posture for Private setups; there are specific contractual and architectural requirements (BAs, encrypted-at-rest KMS integration). We'll include the compliance doc.
[06:33] [06:33] Carlos: Back to perf - I want to call out two gotchas we see: 1) naively increasing context length without changing attention/kv strategy leads to linear or worse cost growth. 2) batch conflation: mixing high-latency long-context requests with short interactive requests in the same queue will bloat tail latencies. Use separate routes/models and QoS routing.
[06:54] Tara: QoS routing - can Redwood route by request metadata like tenant or route tag?
[06:58] Carlos: Yep. You can set policies to route by tenant, route, latency sensitivity. Also automatic fallback to smaller model variants or cached responses if capacity constrained.
[07:09] Rajiv: For bench runs, what inputs do you need from us?
[07:13] Carlos: Ideally: 1) canonical prompt set (Tara will send), 2) representative doc sizes and chunking strategy, 3) model choice, 4) target latency/cost SLOs. We'll run Dedicated env runs and then repeat on your Private env for kernel tuning.
[07:28] Maya: We'll also add notes about expected cost profiles: chunked re-attend has better unit token economics than naive full-attend. Pricing delta for Private/Dedicated vs Hosted we'll include in the follow-up.
[07:41] [07:41] Simone: Are there any live demos or artifacts we can review?
[07:44] Maya: Yes - we'll share a perf spreadsheet, an eval harness link, and a short demo recording of a 128k retrieval flow.
[07:52] Tara: One more: how do you do fallback when KV runs out?
[07:56] Carlos: Multiple layers: 1) fallback to retrieval from embeddings to re-inject context, 2) degrade to summary-only and signal higher uncertainty, 3) route to a higher-capacity Dedicated pool. We surface these as automatic policies in Redwood Console.
[08:12] Rajiv: Any known issues with OpenTelemetry/tracing when doing chunked workloads?
[08:16] Carlos: Traces get more complex when there are many small re-attend calls. We recommend sampling or stiching traces in the Console. We have integrations with common tracing backends.
[08:28] [08:28] Ben: For the on-prem H100s, what's the recommended CUDA stack?
[08:31] Carlos: We'll provide a recommended stack - often CUDA 12.x and tuned NCCL versions; exact versions depend on your distro and driver. We'll pick during the kernel sweep.
[08:42] Maya: quick recap so we have explicit next steps - Carlos, you'll run a perf harness on Redwood Dedicated with Acme prompt set; Maya will send pricing + config; Lina will send quant guides; Ben/Tara will provide the prompt set and success criteria.
[08:55] Carlos: We'll aim to get the initial spreadsheet in 48-72 hours, then schedule the kernel-level session.
[09:02] Tara: sounds good. Thanks everyone.

End of transcript.
